one: A large language model predicts the next token over and over, given everything in its context window. Tokens, context length, sampling and statelessness explain most of its behaviour in your app.
an: An extremely well-read autocomplete with no memory between calls. Every call you hand it the whole conversation again, like briefing a brilliant contractor who forgets everything when they leave the room.
how: Tokens: text is split into sub-word pieces. Pricing, speed and limits are counted in tokens, input and output separately. Non-English text (Korean, Uzbek) often uses more tokens per word, and a new model generation can use a different tokenizer, so the same text can produce a different count.
Context window: the maximum tokens per call (system prompt + history + documents + answer). Anything not in the window does not exist for the model.
Stateless API: chat “memory” is your app resending previous messages. Long chats get slower and costlier per turn unless you trim, summarise or cache.

Sampling: the model picks each next token with some randomness, so the same request can give different answers. Older APIs let you tune this with temperature, but even temperature: 0 never guaranteed identical output, and the newest Claude models reject non-default sampling settings. Steer behaviour with the prompt, examples and structured outputs instead.
Hallucination: the model produces fluent text whether or not it knows; grounding (RAG, tools) and validation reduce it.
why: In 2026 most products ship LLM features. Full-stack seniors are expected to integrate them safely, cheaply and reliably, not just call an API.
trade: Bigger models are smarter, slower and pricier; small fast models are fine for classification and extraction. Route by task.

myth.m: The model remembers our previous conversation.
myth.r: The API remembers nothing. Your code resends history (or a summary) each time.

Each turn resends the full growing history as input tokens
Rate limits
DNS

docs: Andrej Karpathy: Intro to Large Language Models (talk)

plain:
A large language model reads text and predicts what text should come next, one small piece (a token) at a time. Everything it knows about your request must be in the text you send: instructions, history, documents. This is the context window, and it has a size limit.

The API remembers nothing between calls. A chat “remembers” only because your app sends the whole conversation again each time.
bridge: Calling an LLM API is a fetch with your prompt in the body. What surprises frontend developers: it is slow (seconds), it costs money per token, and the same request can give different answers.

walk.title: What happens on turn 10 of a chat
steps: The user types a new question.
Your server builds the request: system instructions + all 9 earlier messages + the new question.
The model reads all of it (input tokens, which you pay for) and generates an answer token by token (output tokens, which cost more).
Your server streams the tokens to the browser so text appears as it is written.
On turn 20, you send even more history. Cost and latency grow every turn unless you trim or summarise older messages.

terms: A small piece of text (part of a word); the unit of pricing and limits.
The maximum tokens one call can include (input plus output).
A sampling setting for how varied the output is. Some newer models no longer accept it.
Fluent, confident output that is not true.
Receiving the answer piece by piece as it is generated.
Why generation ended: finished normally, hit the output cap, wants a tool, or refused.
insights: Chat cost grows with the length of the whole conversation, not only the new message, because every turn resends the history.
The model does not know today's date, your prices or last week's release unless you put them in the context.
Treat the model as a smart but forgetful contractor: everything it needs must be in the brief.

prod.summary: In production an LLM call is a slow, metered, non-deterministic network call. Seniors care about what goes into the context on every turn and how fast it grows, a hard output cap, and code that checks why generation stopped before trusting the text.
checklist: Every call sets an output cap (max_tokens), and code checks the stop reason (Anthropic stop_reason, OpenAI finish_reason). max_tokens / length means truncated output; never treat it as complete.
Token counts are logged from the response usage object (input, output, cached), not estimated from character length.
Large inputs are counted before sending (Anthropic POST /v1/messages/count_tokens) and chunked or rejected with a clear message, not silently truncated.
Chat history has an explicit policy: trim, summarise or compact once it passes a token threshold.
Facts the model cannot know are injected: today's date, the user's plan, current feature list.
The model ID is pinned in config. A model change can change the tokenizer and the accepted parameters, so evals and a smoke test run before the switch.
API keys live only on the server; the browser talks to your endpoint, never to the provider.
numbers: Anthropic's Messages API requires max_tokens on every request; the response usage has input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens.
Anthropic: setting temperature, top_p or top_k to any non-default value on Claude Opus 4.7 and later models returns a 400 error. Omitting them (or leaving the default) is accepted.

Anthropic rate limits are measured per model in requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute (RPM / ITPM / OTPM), enforced with a token bucket, so capacity refills continuously rather than resetting each minute.
Anthropic: a truncated (max_tokens) or refused (refusal) answer still returns HTTP 200. Only the stop_reason field tells you.
failures: Answers end mid-sentence, and JSON.parse fails on a few percent of responses.

Output hit the cap (stop_reason: "max_tokens" / finish_reason: "length") and the code never checked. Check the stop reason on every response, then raise the cap or ask for shorter output. With reasoning models, thinking tokens also use the budget, so a small cap can return almost no visible text.
A chat about a long PDF works for 10 turns, then the API returns 400 “prompt is too long”.

System prompt + history + document exceeded the context window. Count tokens before sending, trim or summarise old turns, and retrieve only the relevant chunks instead of resending the whole document.
The bot states the wrong year, or describes a feature you removed last month.
The model only knows its training data and the context you send. Inject the current date and live product facts from your DB, or ground answers with RAG or tools.
After changing the model ID, every request fails with HTTP 400.
New models can drop parameters (for example, sampling parameters on newer Claude models). Read the provider's migration guide, remove unsupported fields, and run evals before switching traffic.
Cost per user is much higher for Korean users than English users on the same feature.
Non-English text uses more tokens for the same meaning. Measure token counts per language with the provider's counter and budget quotas per language, not per message.

code.title: A production-shaped LLM call: cap, log usage, check stop reason
code.note: The two stop_reason checks are what most first versions miss: a truncated or refused answer still returns HTTP 200.

qs.s: A chat has a 2,000-token system prompt. Each finished turn (user + assistant) adds about 300 tokens to the history, and the new user message is 100 tokens. With no trimming or caching, about how many input tokens does turn 10 send?
qs.e: 2,000 system + 9 earlier turns × 300 + 100 new = 4,800. The prompt is resent in full every turn, so input grows linearly with the conversation and total cost over the whole chat grows roughly quadratically. 2,400 forgets the 9 earlier turns.

qs.s: Your logs show stop_reason: "max_tokens", output_tokens: 1024 and a JSON.parse error for the same request. What is the right first fix?
o: Retry the same request until the JSON parses
Treat max_tokens as an error path: raise the cap or ask for shorter output, and never parse truncated text
Lower the temperature so the JSON is more stable
Switch to a model with a bigger context window
qs.e: The output was cut off at the cap, so the JSON is incomplete. Retrying the same request will usually be cut off again. The context window limits input + output size; it is not the problem here.

qs.s: You upgrade to a newer model ID. Every request now fails with HTTP 400 mentioning temperature. Your code sends temperature: 0 “for determinism”. What should you do?
o: Send temperature: 0.01 instead
Downgrade to the old model permanently
Remove the parameter, steer with clear instructions and a schema, and confirm with your eval set
Set top_p: 0 instead
qs.e: Some newer models reject non-default sampling parameters (for example Claude Opus 4.7 and later). Any non-default value fails, including 0.01 and top_p. Prompt clarity, structured outputs and evals are the supported way to get consistent results.

qs.s: Users say answers sometimes stop mid-sentence, and the next reply “continues” strangely. Read the handler. What is the bug?

code.title: chat.ts

o: History should be stored as a summary, not as full messages
It never checks stop_reason: answers cut off at 300 output tokens are shown and saved to history as if they were complete
The filter drops tool_use blocks, which breaks the next turn
max_tokens includes the input, so long histories leave almost no room for the answer
qs.e: A cut-off answer returns HTTP 200 with stop_reason: "max_tokens". The code treats it as finished, shows it, and stores the broken text in history, which confuses the next turn. On Anthropic's API max_tokens limits only the output; input size is limited by the context window, so “max_tokens includes the input” is the tempting but wrong explanation.

qs.s: A feature handles 10,000 requests a day. Each request has 2,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens. Assume an example price of $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens (not a real price list). What does it cost per day, and which side dominates?
o: $60 a day, almost all input
$27 a day, split evenly
$150 a day, almost all output
$135 a day; output is a quarter of the tokens but more than half the cost
qs.e: Input: 20M tokens × $3/M = $60. Output: 5M tokens × $15/M = $75. Total $135. Output tokens are usually priced several times higher than input, so “shorter answers” is often a bigger saving than “shorter prompts”. $60 forgets the output side.

qs.s: A user writes “My name is Dina”, then “What is my name?”, and the bot says it does not know. Read the endpoint. Why?

code.title: routes/chat.ts

o: The provider's memory feature is turned off for this API key
The sessionId is not sent to the provider, so it cannot find the earlier turn
History is saved in the DB but never sent: the API is stateless, so each call must include the earlier messages
The system prompt is too long, so the model forgot the name
qs.e: The Messages API keeps no state between calls and has no session ID to look things up by. The model only sees what is in messages. Load the session's previous turns from the DB (trimmed to a token budget) and send them with the new message.

qs.s: A teammate estimates monthly LLM cost as “characters ÷ 4 = tokens” for all users. Most of your users write in Uzbek and Korean, and you plan to move to a newer model next quarter. What is the best advice?
o: Use real counts: log usage from every response, and run the provider's token counter on samples per language and per model before switching
The rule is fine; tokenizers are the same across languages and models
Multiply the estimate by 2 for non-English text and keep the rule
Count words instead of characters; words map 1:1 to tokens
qs.e: Token counts per character vary by language and by tokenizer, and a new model generation can change the tokenizer. The response usage object gives real numbers for budgets and dashboards; a counting endpoint lets you re-baseline before a model switch. Any fixed multiplier is a guess that will be wrong for some slice.

interview.q: Walk me through what happens, end to end, when a user sends message 15 in a chat feature built on an LLM API. Where do the latency and cost come from?
answer: The server loads the conversation (or a trimmed/summarised version), adds the system prompt and any retrieved context, and sends all of it as input tokens. The API stores nothing between calls.
Input grows every turn, so cost and time-to-first-token grow too; total cost over a long chat grows roughly quadratically without trimming or caching.
Output is generated token by token; output tokens are slower and priced higher, so max_tokens and the requested length bound the worst case.
Streaming (SSE) hides most of the wait: the user sees text after the first tokens instead of after the full answer.
Production code checks stop_reason (max_tokens, refusal) because both return HTTP 200, logs usage per request, and caches the stable prefix (system prompt, tools) so repeated tokens are cheaper.

Trade-off: keeping full history gives the best answers but the worst cost; summarising old turns is cheap but can lose details, so key facts (name, order ID) are often stored separately and re-injected.
followups: How would you decide when to summarise the history?
What changes if the conversation includes a 100-page PDF?

interview.q: A product manager says the bot gives different answers to the same question and asks you to “turn the randomness off”. What do you tell them, and what do you actually do?
answer: Generation is sampled, so variation is normal. On newer Claude models (Opus 4.7 and later) you cannot set non-default temperature/top_p/top_k at all: the API returns 400. Even temperature: 0 never guaranteed identical outputs on older models.
Ask which kind of difference matters: wording (usually fine) or facts/decisions (a real bug).
For consistent decisions: clearer instructions with reasons, a few varied examples, enums and structured outputs, and grounding facts in the prompt instead of relying on the model's memory.
For identical inputs that must give identical outputs (for example, a cached FAQ answer), cache the response in your own system.
Measure it: run each eval case several times and track how often the decision changes, per slice.
followups: How would you test that a prompt change reduced inconsistency?
When is variation actually useful?

interview.q: Design the chat-history handling for a support bot whose conversations can run to hundreds of turns.
answer: Store the full transcript in your DB; decide per call what to send, based on a token budget measured with real counts, not characters.
Keep the system prompt and tools stable and first so they cache; append new turns at the end so the cached prefix keeps matching.

Past a threshold, replace old turns with a summary, or use the provider's server-side compaction if available; keep key facts (customer ID, order, decisions) in a structured “case state” that is always included.
For details from far back, retrieve relevant old turns on demand instead of sending everything.
Trade-offs: summaries lose detail and cost an extra call; sending everything is accurate but slow and expensive and eventually hits the context window (HTTP 400 “prompt is too long”).
Test it: eval cases that ask about something from turn 5 at turn 80.
followups: How do you stop the summary itself from introducing mistakes?
How does this interact with prompt caching?

one: Prompts are code: versioned, tested against examples, and structured with clear instructions, context, examples and an output format.
an: Writing a brief for a skilled freelancer who has never heard of your company. Vague brief, vague work.
how: Structure: role and goal → context/data (clearly delimited, e.g. XML tags) → rules and constraints → examples (few-shot) → exact output format.
Say what to do, not only what to avoid. Give the reason behind rules; models generalise from reasons.
Keep stable parts (instructions, examples) first so they can be cached; put the changing user input last.
Store prompts in the repo, review changes like code, and run them against a fixed set of test cases (evals) before shipping.
why: Most LLM feature quality comes from the prompt and context, not the model choice. Treating prompts casually makes behaviour drift silently.
trade: Longer prompts cost tokens on every call. Trim what does not change results, measured by evals.

myth.r: It is clear specification plus testing, the same skills as writing a good ticket and a good test suite.

q.s: A summariser sometimes invents details not in the source. Which prompt change helps most?
o: Add 'be accurate'
Delimit the source, instruct to use only facts from it, and to say when something is not stated; then verify with evals
Raise temperature
Shorten the source
q.e: Clear grounding rules plus measurement beat vague adjectives.

lab: Take one prompt from a project you built. Write 15 test inputs (normal, edge, adversarial) with expected properties. Change the prompt three times and score each version on the set.

plain:
A prompt is the instructions and context you give the model. Good prompts read like a clear brief: the goal, the context, the rules, a few examples, and the exact output format.

Treat prompts like code: keep them in the repo, review changes, and test them on a fixed set of examples before shipping.
bridge: Writing a good prompt is like writing a good ticket for a new teammate who is very capable but knows nothing about your project. Vague ticket, vague result.

walk.title: Improving a support-reply prompt
steps: Version 1: “Reply to this customer email.” Replies are long, sometimes promise refunds you do not offer.
Add context: who you are, your refund policy in <policy> tags, the customer's order data in <order> tags.
Add rules with reasons: “Never promise refunds outside the policy, because support cannot honour them.”
Add two short example replies in your tone, and the format: “Under 120 words, no greeting longer than one line.”
Run all versions on 20 saved real emails and compare. Version 4 wins clearly, measured, not guessed.

terms: Including examples of input and desired output.
Tags or markers separating instructions from data.
A saved, tracked version of a prompt.
insights: Explaining why a rule exists works better than shouting the rule.
Models copy examples closely, including their length and tone, so make examples look exactly like the output you want.
Without a test set, every prompt change is a guess.

prod.summary: In production a prompt is configuration that changes behaviour for every user at once. Seniors version it, log the version with every request, keep untrusted data clearly separated from instructions, keep the stable part byte-identical so it caches, and never merge a prompt change without running the eval set.
checklist: The prompt lives in the repo (or a prompt registry), and its version ID is logged with every request so you can trace a bad answer to the exact prompt.
Untrusted input (emails, documents, web pages) is wrapped in tags like <email>, and the prompt says that content is data, not instructions.
The stable part (system prompt, tool definitions, examples) comes first and is identical on every call: no timestamps, user names or request IDs in it.
Rules come with a reason, and rules do not contradict each other (“be brief” and “explain every step”).
Few-shot examples are short and varied. Models copy examples closely: their length, tone and even names.
The output format is enforced by code (structured outputs, schema validation), not only by “respond in JSON”.
The eval set runs in CI on every prompt change, with results per category, not just one average.
numbers: Anthropic prompt caching: any byte change in the prefix invalidates the cache from that point on; render order is tools → system → messages.
Anthropic: the minimum cacheable prefix is 512 to 4,096 tokens depending on the model. A shorter prefix silently does not cache (no error, cache_creation_input_tokens: 0).
A cache entry lives 5 minutes by default (1 hour optional) on Anthropic, and each read refreshes the timer.
failures: After someone adds “Today is {date} {time}” to the system prompt, cache_read_input_tokens drops to 0 and latency rises.
Dynamic text inside the cached prefix changes the bytes on every request. Move the date to the user turn (after the cache breakpoint) or round it to the day.
Every reply opens with “Great question!” and is three times longer than you asked for.

The examples or tone instructions contradict the length rule, or the examples themselves are long. Make examples the exact target length and state the format positively (“under 80 words, plain text”).
A prompt fix for one customer complaint breaks refund answers for everyone else.
No regression test set. Add cases for each category, run them in CI, and review prompt diffs like code.
The model follows instructions written inside a customer's uploaded document.

Data and instructions are mixed. Wrap untrusted content in tags and say it is data. This lowers the risk but does not remove it; real protection comes from limiting what the model can do (see LLM security).
An old prompt full of “CRITICAL: you MUST…” makes a newer model refuse harmless requests or call a tool on every turn.
Newer models follow instructions more literally, so shouted rules over-trigger. Remove the emphasis, explain the reason for the rule, and re-run evals.

code.title: A versioned prompt: stable part first, untrusted data tagged
code.note: The system prompt has no dynamic values, so it can be cached. Customer text sits inside <email> and the prompt says it is data.

qs.s: Prompt caching is enabled, but cache_read_input_tokens is always 0. The system prompt starts with You are SupportBot. Request ID: ${requestId}. followed by 5,000 tokens of policy. What is wrong?
o: The policy is too long to cache
Caching only works with temperature 0
Caching needs at least 10 requests per minute
The request ID changes the first bytes every time, so no two prompts share a prefix
qs.e: Caching matches an exact prefix. A value that changes per request at the start breaks the match for everything after it. Move the ID out of the prompt (or to the end). 5,000 tokens is above every model's minimum.

qs.s: A classifier prompt has 3 examples, all about billing. In production, the model labels many unclear tickets as “billing”. What is the most likely cause and fix?
o: The examples biased the model; use varied examples that cover each category and an “other” case
The model is too small; use a bigger one
Temperature is too low; raise it
The tickets are too long; truncate them
qs.e: Models copy the pattern of the examples. Three billing examples teach “answer billing”. Balanced, varied examples (plus a clear rule for unsure cases) fix the bias; check it with per-category eval scores.

qs.s: Two prompt versions on 200 eval cases: v1 scores 90% overall, v2 scores 92% overall but drops the “legal” slice from 95% to 70% (20 cases). What do you do?
o: Ship v2; the average went up
Do not ship v2 yet; find why the legal cases fail, fix the prompt, and re-run before shipping
Ship v2 and add a note to monitor legal tickets
Run v2 again; it is just noise
qs.e: A 25-point drop on 20 cases is 5 extra failures in a sensitive category, which is not noise. Averages hide slice regressions; the eval exists to block exactly this.

qs.s: This prompt diff was merged to fix answers that were too long. Afterwards, the assistant calls the search tool even for “thanks!”, and p50 latency doubles. What is the most likely cause and fix?

code.title: prompts/support.txt (diff)
code.src:
- Answer in under 100 words.
+ IMPORTANT!!! You MUST ALWAYS answer in under 100 words. NEVER exceed this.
+ ALWAYS use the search tool before answering ANY message.
  Use the customer's language.

o: The search tool is slow; add a cache in front of it
The model ignores capital letters, so the change had no effect

Newer models follow instructions literally: “ALWAYS … ANY message” makes it search on every turn. State when search helps and why (“search when the question is about orders or policy, because…”), then re-run evals
Under 100 words is too short; the model searches to fill the space
qs.e: Shouted absolute rules over-trigger on models that follow instructions closely. A rule with a reason and a scope (“when the user asks about X, because Y”) lets the model generalise. Caching the tool hides the symptom but still pays a tool round on every turn.

qs.s: Pro and free users get different tool lists. A teammate expects one shared cached system prompt for everyone. Read the request. What actually happens?

code.title: ask.ts

o: One shared cache entry: cache_control is on the system block, so tools do not matter
Each tool list gives a different cache prefix, because tools render before the system prompt. Use one deterministic tool list for everyone and enforce plan limits inside the tool handlers
Caching is turned off whenever tools are present
Only the messages part is affected; the system prompt is always shared
qs.e: Anthropic renders tools → system → messages, and a cache hit needs a byte-identical prefix. A change in tool definitions invalidates everything after it, so each plan builds its own cache. Enforcing the plan in the handler also keeps the security check in code, where it belongs.

qs.s: Your support prompt has two example replies, both to a customer named Anna. In production, about 2% of replies greet the customer as “Anna”. What is the best fix?
o: Add “Do not use the name Anna” to the rules
Remove all examples
Raise the model tier so it understands examples better
Use several varied examples with different names and situations, wrap them in <example> tags, and say they show style, not content
qs.e: Models copy examples closely, including names, length and tone. Varied examples teach the pattern instead of the details. A “don't say Anna” rule patches one symptom; removing examples loses the tone guidance that made them useful.

qs.s: Your system prompt is 9,000 tokens. Cache hit rate is 95%. A teammate wants to cut it to 3,000 tokens “to save money”. What should you do first?
o: Measure: with a 95% hit rate most of those tokens are already billed at the cache-read rate. Compute the real saving from usage, and only cut sections that the eval set shows do not change results
Cut it today; fewer tokens always means lower cost and better answers
Never shorten a working prompt
Move the prompt into the user message so it is not cached
qs.e: Cached prefix tokens cost a small fraction of the normal input price, so the saving may be small, while removed rules can silently break slices. Decide with both numbers: real cost from usage and quality from evals.

interview.q: How do you manage prompts in a production codebase where several engineers change them?
answer: Prompts live in the repo (or a registry backed by it), with a version ID logged on every request, so any bad answer traces to an exact prompt, model ID and config.
Changes go through PR review like code; reviewers read the diff and the eval report together.
An eval set runs in CI on every prompt change, scored per slice (category, language), with a gate on the worst slice, not the average.
Stable parts are kept byte-identical (no timestamps or user names) so caching keeps working; volatile data goes in the user turn.
Risky changes roll out behind a flag or to a percentage of traffic, with online metrics (escalations, thumbs-down) watched.
Trade-off: a separate prompt-management UI lets non-engineers edit, but without tests and review it becomes an unreviewed production deploy.
followups: How would you let the support team suggest prompt changes safely?
What do you log so a bad answer can be reproduced?

interview.q: A prompt works well on the current model. You are moving to a newer model. What do you check before switching traffic?
answer: API changes from the migration guide: for example, on newer Claude models non-default sampling parameters and assistant-message prefill return 400; replace prefill with structured outputs or instructions.
Behaviour changes: newer models follow instructions more literally, so emphatic rules (“MUST”, “ALWAYS”) can over-trigger; remove the shouting and give reasons.
Tokenizer and cost: re-count tokens on real samples, because the same text can produce a different count.
Run the full eval set on both models, compare per slice, and read the flipped cases, not just the score.
Canary a small share of traffic and compare online signals before the full switch; keep the old model ID ready for rollback.
followups: What would make you keep the old model for one route?
How long do you run the canary?

interview.q: How do you keep untrusted content (emails, documents, web pages) from steering the model, and where does prompting stop being enough?
answer: Put untrusted text in clearly named tags (<email>, <source>) and say in the system prompt that it is data, not instructions.
Keep operator instructions in the system prompt (or the provider's system channel), never mixed into the same string as user data.
This lowers the success rate of injection but cannot guarantee anything: a model can still be persuaded.

Real protection is capability-based: flows that read untrusted content get no dangerous tools, side effects need user confirmation, tool handlers authorise as the user, and output is escaped before rendering.
Test it: a red-team set of injected documents runs with the evals.
followups: Would a second “guard” model solve this?
How do you handle data exfiltration through links?

one: When code consumes model output, ask for JSON matching a schema, use the provider's structured-output or tool features where available, and always validate before use.
an: Asking a person to fill in a form instead of writing a letter, then still checking the form before filing it.
how: Describe the schema in the prompt or pass it via the API's structured output / tool-use mechanism, which constrains the format.
Parse and validate with Zod (or similar). On failure: retry once with the validation error, or fall back.
Keep schemas small and flat; use enums for categories; allow "unknown"/null instead of forcing a guess.
Never pass model output straight into SQL, shell, eval or HTML.
why: Extraction, classification, routing and agents all depend on machine-readable output. Unvalidated output is a reliability and security bug.
trade: Strict schemas can lower answer quality on hard reasoning tasks, because the model must commit to an answer in a fixed shape. Let it think first: use the model's built-in thinking, or put a required reasoning field before the decision field. Do not make that field optional: Anthropic structured outputs generate required properties before optional ones, so an optional reasoning field would come after the decision and not help it.

myth.m: With structured outputs turned on, I can trust the result without checks.
myth.r: Schema enforcement guarantees the shape, not the values. A refusal or a hit on max_tokens can still break the format, and a valid enum can still be the wrong category. Check the stop reason and apply business rules.

q.s: An LLM classifies support tickets into 5 categories and sometimes returns a 6th made-up category, crashing a switch statement. Fix?
o: Ask it nicely
Use an enum in the schema, validate with Zod, and map invalid output to 'other' or retry
Raise max_tokens
Use a bigger model only
q.e: Constrain, validate, and handle failure explicitly.

more: Provider structured outputs vs JSON mode
lab: Build an endpoint that extracts {name, phone, date, intent} from free text using a schema; validate with Zod; log failure rate over 50 varied inputs.
docs: Anthropic: Tool use (structured output via tools)

plain: When your code (not a human) uses the model's answer, ask for structured data, usually JSON matching a schema. Many APIs can enforce a schema (structured outputs or tool use). Always validate the result in your code before using it.
bridge: Same rule as any API response: parse it with Zod before trusting it. An LLM is just a less predictable API.

walk.title: Classifying support tickets
steps: Schema: { category: 'billing' | 'bug' | 'account' | 'other', urgency: 'low' | 'normal' | 'high', summary: string }.
Pass the schema through the provider's structured-output feature (or a strict tool). The model's decoding is constrained, so the reply always matches the shape.
Without that feature (plain “reply in JSON”), parse with Zod: most replies pass, but at volume some are off-schema every day (e.g. category “refund”). Retry once with the validation error.
Either way, check the stop reason: a refusal or a cut-off at max_tokens can still produce unusable output.
Still unusable: set category to “other” and flag for a human. The system never crashes on bad output.

terms: Model output constrained to a schema.
A description of the shape JSON must have.
Checking output against the schema in your code.
What to do when output is unusable.
insights: Never pass model output directly into SQL, shell commands or HTML.
Enums and “unknown” options make the model's job easier and your data cleaner.
At high volume, rare format failures happen every day; count them and plan the fallback.

prod.summary: Structured output is how LLMs plug into code: classifiers, extractors, routers, agents. In production seniors use the provider's schema enforcement where available, still validate in code, plan a fallback for refusals and truncation, and treat every field as untrusted input.
checklist: Use provider-enforced schemas (structured outputs / strict tools) instead of “please reply in JSON” wherever the provider supports it.
Validate with Zod (or similar) at the boundary anyway: it gives you types and catches the cases enforcement does not cover.
Check the stop reason before parsing: refusal and max_tokens can break the schema even with enforcement.
Categories are enums with an “other” / “unknown” option; nullable fields instead of forced guesses.
The schema uses only features the provider supports (many reject numeric min/max, string length limits or recursive schemas).
Every field is treated as untrusted: parameterised SQL, escaped HTML, allow-listed values before any side effect.
Track the fallback rate per day; a jump means a prompt, model or input change.
numbers: Anthropic structured outputs: JSON outputs via output_config.format and strict tool use via strict: true; the older output_format parameter is deprecated.

Anthropic structured outputs do not support recursive schemas, numeric constraints (minimum, maximum), string length constraints, and require additionalProperties: false on objects. The TypeScript and Python SDK helpers remove unsupported constraints from the schema they send and validate them locally (Zod / Pydantic); a raw JSON schema with them is rejected.
Anthropic compiles each new schema into a grammar on first use (extra latency) and caches it for 24 hours from last use; changing the schema structure or the tool set invalidates it.
Anthropic limits per request, across all strict schemas combined: 20 strict tools, 24 optional parameters, 16 parameters with union types (anyOf or type arrays).
Anthropic: in structured output, required properties appear first, then optional ones, not in schema order.
failures: Extraction works in tests, but production logs show a few ZodErrors every hour.

The code asks for JSON in the prompt but does not use schema enforcement, so off-schema replies appear at volume. Switch to structured outputs / strict tools, keep validation, and route failures to a fallback.
With structured outputs on, some calls still throw Failed to parse structured output.

Those responses ended with stop_reason refusal or max_tokens, where the schema is not guaranteed, or returned an enum value the grammar did not enforce (the TS SDK helper moves enum, minimum and maximum into the description, and Zod rejects them after parsing). The SDK's parse() throws instead of returning, so catch that error and use the fallback; raise the cap or handle the refusal path.
The API returns 400 after adding minimum: 1, maximum: 3 to a hand-written JSON schema.

Enforced schemas do not support numeric constraints. Use an enum ('low' | 'normal' | 'high'), or define the schema in Zod and use the SDK helper, which strips the constraint from what it sends and checks it after parsing.
A support dashboard shows a script running in an agent's browser.
A model-extracted summary field was rendered as HTML. Structured does not mean safe: escape every field before rendering, like any user input.
The first request with a new schema is several seconds slower than the rest.
Grammar compilation on first use. Expected; it is cached afterwards. Warm it at deploy time if the first-request latency matters.

code.title: Schema-enforced classification with a safe fallback
code.note: The schema's shape (keys, types, required) is enforced during generation; enum values and ranges are checked by Zod after parsing. parse() throws on cut-off or rejected JSON, so the catch and the stop-reason check send every bad case to the fallback.

qs.s: You pass a hand-written JSON schema in output_config.format with "age": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 120 }. Requests now fail with HTTP 400. What is the best fix?
o: Drop structured outputs and ask for JSON in the prompt
Change age to a string
Remove minimum/maximum from the schema you send and check the range in your own validation (the SDK's Zod helper does exactly this for you)
Add “age must be 0 to 120” in capital letters to the prompt
qs.e: Enforced schemas do not support numeric constraints, so a raw schema that contains them is rejected. Send the simpler schema for generation and keep the business check in code. Dropping enforcement loses the shape guarantee.

qs.s: With structured outputs enabled, 0.3% of responses still fail to parse. Logs show stop_reason: "max_tokens" on all of them. What do you do?
o: Nothing; 0.3% is acceptable noise
Report a bug to the provider
Turn off structured outputs
Raise max_tokens (or shorten the requested output) and handle max_tokens as an explicit error path
qs.e: Enforcement cannot finish a JSON object that was cut off at the output cap. The fix is a bigger cap or a smaller output, and code that never parses a truncated response.

qs.s: An LLM extracts { refund_amount: number } from customer emails and your code issues refunds automatically. The schema is enforced. What is still missing?
o: Business validation: the amount must be ≤ the order total and within policy, with human approval above a threshold
Nothing; the schema guarantees a number
A bigger model
A second LLM call to double-check the JSON format
qs.e: A schema guarantees a number, not the right number. An email can say “refund me $5,000” (or contain injected text). Money-moving values need business rules and approval, enforced in code.

qs.s: The team wanted the model to reason before deciding, so they put reasoning first in the schema. Reviewers notice the reasoning often reads like a justification written after the fact. Why?

code.title: verdict.ts

o: Zod sorts object keys alphabetically, so decision comes first
Nothing is wrong; JSON key order does not matter
Structured outputs generate required properties before optional ones, so decision is written before reasoning. Make reasoning required (and first) or rely on the model's built-in thinking
max_tokens is too low, so the reasoning is cut short
qs.e: Generation order is the order the model “thinks” in. Anthropic's docs state that required properties come first, then optional ones. With an optional reasoning field, the decision is already fixed when the reasoning is written. Key order does not matter to JSON.parse, but it matters to generation.

qs.s: The schema is enforced and customer_name is always a string. Read the code. What is wrong?

code.title: extract.ts

o: Nothing: the schema guarantees a plain string
The model may return the name in a different case
$queryRawUnsafe is slow; use a view

Two bugs: the value comes from untrusted email text, so string-built SQL allows injection (use a parameterised query); and nothing handles refusal or max_tokens: parsed_output can be null (so ! lies), and parse() throws on cut-off JSON
qs.e: A schema guarantees type, not safety: an email containing x' OR '1'='1 produces a perfectly valid string. Treat every field like user input: parameterise SQL, escape HTML. Also handle the failure paths: catch the error parse() throws when the JSON is cut off, and check stop_reason before trusting parsed_output.

qs.s: A request uses 8 strict tools with 4 optional parameters each, plus a JSON output schema with 2 optional fields. Anthropic returns 400. What is the cause?
o: More than 5 strict tools per request is not allowed

34 optional parameters in total is over the limit of 24 across all strict schemas in one request; make some fields required (with an “unknown” value), split tools across requests, or drop strict on low-risk tools
Each tool may have at most 3 optional parameters
Structured outputs cannot be combined with tools in one request
qs.e: 8 × 4 + 2 = 34. Anthropic's limit is 24 optional parameters combined across every strict tool and output schema in the request (and 20 strict tools). Making fields nullable with ["string", "null"] uses union types, which have their own limit of 16.

qs.s: This code reserves stock using a quantity extracted by the model. Production shows a reservation of 0 and one of 500. Why?

code.title: reserve.ts

o: The SDK removes minimum/maximum from the schema it sends, and this JSON-schema helper does not validate the response, so nothing enforces 1–10. Check the range in code before reserving
The model ignored the schema; report a bug to the provider
integer is not supported; use number
The values come from a stale grammar cache
qs.e: Per Anthropic's docs, the TypeScript jsonSchemaOutputFormat() helper transforms unsupported constraints by default and, unlike the Zod helper, does not validate the response. The shape is guaranteed (an integer), but the range is not. Money and stock decisions need an explicit check in code.

interview.q: Design an LLM extractor that turns 50,000 free-text invoices a day into rows in Postgres. How do you make it reliable?
answer: Provider-enforced schema (structured outputs) with enums and nullable/“unknown” fields instead of forced guesses; the schema stays small and flat.
Validate with Zod at the boundary for types plus business rules (totals add up, dates in range, currency in allow-list).
Check stop_reason first: refusal or max_tokens means the output may not match the schema; route to retry or a human queue.
Idempotent writes keyed by invoice ID; parameterised SQL; every field treated as untrusted.
Non-urgent volume goes through a batch API (cheaper); results are matched by custom ID, not position.
Track fallback rate and field-level accuracy against a labelled sample per supplier/format; a jump means a prompt, model or input change.
followups: How do you handle a new invoice layout you have never seen?
Which fields would you double-check with rules instead of trusting the model?

interview.q: Structured outputs, “please reply in JSON”, and tool calling for structure: when do you use which?
answer: Structured outputs (output_config.format) when the whole response is data for code: guaranteed shape, no parsing retries.
Strict tool use when the model should decide whether and which action to take, with arguments guaranteed to match the schema.
Prompt-only JSON only where enforcement is not available; then validate, retry once with the error, and fall back.
Old pattern of forcing a single tool to get JSON: some newest models reject forced tool_choice with 400, so structured outputs is the replacement.

Limits to design around: unsupported constraints (min/max, lengths, recursion), per-request complexity limits, first-use compilation latency, and incompatibility with some features (Anthropic citations).
followups: How would you stream a structured response to a UI?
What happens to quality on a hard reasoning task with a strict schema?

interview.q: The model's output passes schema validation but is wrong. How do you catch and handle that?
answer: Accept that shape ≠ correctness: a valid enum can be the wrong category, a valid number the wrong amount.
Business rules in code: cross-check against source data (order total, customer's real orders), ranges, allow-lists.
Risk-based handling: low-risk fields auto-apply; money, deletes or legal outcomes need approval above a threshold.
Let the model abstain: an “unknown”/“needs_review” option is cheaper than a confident wrong guess.
Measure field accuracy on a labelled set per slice, and sample production outputs for human review weekly.
followups: Would asking the model for a confidence score help?
How do you pick the approval threshold?

one: An embedding turns text (or images) into a vector of numbers where similar meanings are close together. Vector search finds the nearest ones.
an: Placing every sentence on a giant map where "car broke down" lands near "vehicle won't start" even though they share no words.
how: An embedding model maps text → e.g. 1,024 numbers. Similarity is measured with cosine similarity or dot product.
Store vectors in a vector index: pgvector in Postgres, or dedicated stores (Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate). Approximate indexes (HNSW, IVFFlat) trade a little accuracy for speed.
Use cases: semantic search, RAG retrieval, deduplication, clustering, recommendations.
Hybrid search (keyword BM25 + vectors) usually beats either alone, especially for names, codes and exact terms.
why: Retrieval quality decides RAG quality. Understanding embeddings lets you debug "why did it fetch the wrong document?"
trade: Changing embedding models means re-embedding everything. Vectors are poor at exact matches (IDs, numbers) and negation.

myth.r: It complements it. Exact terms, product codes and rare names still need keyword matching.

q.s: Searching an internal wiki for error code "E4021" returns vaguely related pages but not the one containing the code. Why, and fix?
o: Embeddings are broken
Embeddings capture meaning, not exact tokens; add keyword search and combine (hybrid)
Use a bigger vector size
Lower temperature
q.e: Exact identifiers are a keyword-search strength.

more: Cosine vs dot product vs L2
lab: Enable pgvector in local Postgres, embed 200 short documents with any embedding API, and run nearest-neighbour queries.
Add a Postgres full-text query and merge both result lists with reciprocal rank fusion. Compare on 10 test questions.

plain:
An embedding turns a piece of text into a long list of numbers (a vector) that represents its meaning. Texts with similar meaning get vectors that are close to each other, even when they use different words.

Vector search finds the stored texts whose vectors are closest to your question's vector.
bridge: Keyword search finds “car won't start” only if those words appear. Vector search also finds “vehicle fails to turn on”. It is what powers “search by meaning” and most RAG systems.

walk.title: Searching help articles by meaning
steps: Offline: split 500 help articles into paragraphs and get an embedding for each from an embedding API. Store them in Postgres with pgvector.
A user asks: “why was I charged twice?”
Get the embedding of the question.
Query: the 5 stored paragraphs with the closest vectors. Top result: “Duplicate payments and how refunds work”, which never uses the word “charged”.
Combine with keyword search so exact terms like error codes are still found.

terms: A vector of numbers representing meaning.
A list of numbers; here, hundreds or thousands long.
A common measure of how close two vectors are.
A Postgres extension for storing and searching vectors.
Keyword search and vector search combined.
insights: Vectors are weak at exact matches (codes, names, numbers); combine with keyword search.
Changing the embedding model means re-embedding everything.
Retrieval quality usually matters more than which LLM you use.

prod.summary: In production, embeddings are a data pipeline: every document is chunked, embedded with one specific model, and indexed. Seniors care about recall (did the right chunk come back?), filtering by tenant and permissions, keeping the embedding model and index in sync, and combining vectors with keyword search.
checklist: The embedding model name and dimension are stored with every vector; queries and documents always use the same model.
Re-embedding is planned as a migration (new column or table, backfill, switch reads), because a model change makes old vectors useless.
The index opclass matches the distance you query with (e.g. pgvector vector_cosine_ops with <=>), or the index is not used.
Filtered queries (tenant, permissions) are tested for recall: approximate indexes filter after the scan and can return too few rows.
Hybrid search (keyword + vector) is in place for codes, names and exact terms.
Recall@k is measured on a labelled question set before and after changing chunking, model or index settings.
For retrieval models that support it, queries and documents are embedded with the right input type (e.g. Voyage input_type “query” vs “document”).
numbers: pgvector (v0.8.x): vector stores up to 16,000 dimensions, but HNSW and IVFFlat indexes support up to 2,000 (halfvec up to 4,000).
pgvector HNSW defaults: m = 16, ef_construction = 64, query-time hnsw.ef_search = 40. IVFFlat default ivfflat.probes = 1; start with lists = rows / 1000 up to 1M rows.
pgvector operators: <-> L2 distance, <#> negative inner product, <=> cosine distance.
Anthropic does not offer its own embedding model; its docs point to Voyage AI, whose current general models default to 1,024 dimensions (256, 512, 2,048 optional).
Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) commonly uses the constant k = 60: score = Σ 1 / (60 + rank).
failures: A tenant-filtered vector query with LIMIT 10 returns only 2 rows, though the tenant has thousands of documents.

The HNSW index returns the top ef_search (default 40) candidates first, then the WHERE filter removes most of them. Enable hnsw.iterative_scan (pgvector 0.8+), raise ef_search, or partition / partially index per tenant.
After switching embedding providers, search returns nonsense.
Queries are embedded with the new model but stored vectors came from the old one; the spaces are not comparable. Re-embed everything into a new column, backfill, then switch reads.
CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw fails for a 3,072-dimension column.
pgvector indexes support up to 2,000 dimensions for vector. Use a model or setting with ≤ 2,000 dimensions, or store as halfvec (index limit 4,000).
EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan on the vector query and p95 latency is seconds.
The query operator does not match the index opclass (e.g. index built with vector_l2_ops, query uses <=> cosine), or there is no ORDER BY ... LIMIT. Match operator and opclass.
Searches for “E4021” or a customer's name return vaguely related pages.
Embeddings capture meaning, not exact strings. Add keyword search (Postgres full-text with the simple config keeps codes intact) and merge with RRF.

code.title: pgvector hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion
code.src:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE chunks (
  id        bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id bigint NOT NULL,
  body      text   NOT NULL,
  embedding vector(1024) NOT NULL,   -- must equal the embedding model's dimension
  tsv       tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('simple', body)) STORED
);
-- HNSW defaults: m = 16, ef_construction = 64. Use the opclass that matches your distance.
CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING gin (tsv);
CREATE INDEX ON chunks (tenant_id);

-- Per query (inside a transaction): $1 = query vector, $2 = query text, $3 = tenant
SET LOCAL hnsw.ef_search = 100;                 -- default 40: higher = better recall, slower
SET LOCAL hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order;  -- keep scanning when WHERE removes rows

WITH semantic AS (
  SELECT id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY embedding <=> $1) AS r
  FROM chunks WHERE tenant_id = $3
  ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 40
), keyword AS (
  SELECT id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(tsv, q) DESC) AS r
  FROM chunks, websearch_to_tsquery('simple', $2) AS q
  WHERE tenant_id = $3 AND tsv @@ q
  ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(tsv, q) DESC LIMIT 40
)
SELECT c.id, c.body,
       COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + s.r), 0) + COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + k.r), 0) AS rrf_score
FROM semantic s
FULL OUTER JOIN keyword k USING (id)
JOIN chunks c USING (id)
ORDER BY rrf_score DESC
LIMIT 8;
code.note: The FULL OUTER JOIN keeps chunks found by only one method; hnsw.iterative_scan stops the tenant filter from starving the vector results.

qs.s: You store 1,000,000 chunks as vector(1024) with float4 values (4 bytes each). Roughly how much space do the raw vectors take, before any index?
o: About 400 MB
About 4 GB
About 4 MB
About 40 GB
qs.e: 1,000,000 × 1,024 × 4 bytes ≈ 4.1 GB. The HNSW index adds more on top. This is why teams use smaller dimensions, halfvec (2 bytes) or quantisation at scale.

qs.s: A vector query WHERE tenant_id = 42 ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 10 often returns fewer than 10 rows. Tenant 42 is 1% of the table. What is happening?
o: The cosine operator is wrong
The index is corrupted and needs REINDEX
The approximate index returns its top ~40 candidates, then the filter removes most of them; enable iterative scans or raise ef_search
Postgres limits vector queries to the first page
qs.e: With approximate indexes, filtering happens after the index scan. With a 1% tenant, almost all 40 default candidates are from other tenants. pgvector 0.8 iterative scans keep reading the index until enough rows pass the filter.

qs.s: Your team wants to switch to a better embedding model. 5 million chunks are embedded with the current one. What is a safe rollout?
o: Embed only new documents with the new model
Switch the query embedding today; old vectors still work
Average the old and new vectors
Add a new vector column, backfill it with the new model, compare recall on an eval set, then switch reads and drop the old column
qs.e: Vectors from different models live in different spaces, so mixing them breaks similarity. Treat it like a schema migration: backfill in parallel, measure, then switch.

qs.s: Read the index definition and the plan. Why is the vector query slow?

code.title: psql

o: HNSW indexes only work after VACUUM ANALYZE
LIMIT 10 is too small for the planner to choose the index
The table is too large for HNSW; switch to IVFFlat
The query uses <-> (L2 distance) but the index was built for cosine (vector_cosine_ops); query with <=> or build an L2 index
qs.e: In pgvector, an index serves only the operator of its opclass: vector_cosine_ops ↔ <=>, vector_l2_ops ↔ <->, vector_ip_ops ↔ <#>. With a mismatch, Postgres falls back to a sequential scan and a sort over every row.

qs.s: You have 2,000,000 chunks stored as vector(1536) (4 bytes per dimension). How much raw storage do you save by switching to halfvec(1536) (2 bytes per dimension), before indexes?
o: About 6 GB (from about 12.3 GB to about 6.1 GB)
About 600 MB
About 12 GB
Nothing; Postgres compresses vectors automatically
qs.e: 2,000,000 × 1,536 × 4 B ≈ 12.3 GB; with 2 bytes ≈ 6.1 GB, so about 6 GB saved, and the HNSW index shrinks too. halfvec also raises pgvector's index limit from 2,000 to 4,000 dimensions. Measure recall@k after the change: lower precision can cost a little accuracy.

qs.s: Search quality has slowly got worse over two weeks, mostly for documents that were edited recently. Read the nightly job. What is the most likely cause?

code.title: jobs/reembed.ts

o: The HNSW index needs a REINDEX after updates

Edited documents are now embedded with a different model than the queries and the other documents; vectors from different models are not comparable. Store the model name per row and migrate everything at once
Updating vectors in place fragments the table
The new model is worse; switch back and the problem disappears
qs.e: Each embedding model defines its own vector space. Mixing models gives similarity scores that mean nothing, and the damage grows as more documents are edited. Treat a model change as a migration: new column, full backfill, compare recall, then switch queries and documents together.

qs.s: A table gets thousands of new chunks per hour and needs high recall. A teammate wants to create an IVFFlat index now, while the table is still nearly empty, “so it is ready”. What do you recommend?
o: IVFFlat, created now: it adapts its clusters as rows arrive
No index; sequential scans are fine at any size

HNSW: better speed–recall trade-off and no training step, at the cost of slower builds and more memory. IVFFlat computes its lists from the rows present at build time, so building it on an empty table gives poor recall
IVFFlat with lists = 1 so it never needs rebuilding
qs.e: pgvector's docs recommend creating IVFFlat after the table has data, because the cluster centres come from existing rows and are not updated later. HNSW has no training step, which suits constant inserts; plan for its build time and memory.

interview.q: How would you build semantic search over 10 million help articles in Postgres, and what breaks first as it grows?
answer: Chunk by structure (headings, paragraphs), store chunk text, metadata (tenant, ACL, updated_at), model name and vector; pgvector HNSW with the opclass matching the query operator.
Hybrid search: Postgres full-text (or BM25) plus vectors, merged with reciprocal rank fusion, because codes and names need exact matches.

What breaks first: memory and build time of the HNSW index, filtered queries returning too few rows (fix with iterative scans, higher ef_search, partitioning or partial indexes per tenant), and storage (halfvec or fewer dimensions).
Measure recall@k on a labelled question set before and after every change to chunking, model or index settings.
Trade-off: a dedicated vector DB scales further and filters better, but adds a second store to keep in sync with permissions and deletes; Postgres keeps one source of truth.
followups: When would you move off pgvector?
How do you handle deletes and permission changes?

interview.q: How do you know whether your vector search is good? What exactly do you measure?
answer: A labelled set of real queries with the chunk(s) that should come back, including hard cases: codes, names, negation, other languages.
Recall@k (did the right chunk appear in the top k?) and MRR or nDCG (how high did it rank?), reported per slice.
Compare variants on the same set: chunk size, overlap, model, hybrid vs vector-only, re-ranker on/off, ef_search.
Online: click-through or “answer helped” rates, and queries with no good result, which become new test cases.
Also latency (p95) and cost, because a 1% recall gain is not worth doubling p95 for every query.
followups: How many labelled queries do you need?
How do you label without a big annotation team?

interview.q: We need to switch embedding providers. Plan the migration.
answer: Compare first: embed a sample, run the labelled recall set on both models, check dimensions against index limits (pgvector indexes: 2,000 for vector, 4,000 for halfvec).
Add a new vector column (or table) tagged with the model name; backfill in batches with rate limiting and resumable progress.
New and edited documents are written to both columns during the backfill so nothing is missed.
Build the new index, compare recall and latency on the eval set, then switch query embedding and search to the new column in one release.
Keep the old column for quick rollback, then drop it; never mix vectors from two models in one similarity search.
followups: How long would 50 million chunks take to backfill, and what limits it?
How do you test the switch in production safely?

one: Fetch the relevant pieces of your own data at question time, put them in the prompt, and have the model answer from them, ideally with citations.
an: An open-book exam: instead of hoping the student memorised the textbook, you hand them the right three pages for each question.
how: Ingest: split documents into chunks (by headings/paragraphs), add metadata (source, date, section), embed, store.
Retrieve: embed the question, run hybrid search, filter by metadata and permissions, optionally re-rank, take the top few chunks.
Generate: prompt with the chunks clearly delimited, instruct to answer only from them and cite sources, and to say "not found" otherwise.
Evaluate retrieval (did the right chunk come back?) separately from generation (was the answer faithful?).
why: It is the standard way to make LLMs answer about private, fresh or domain-specific data without retraining. A very common senior full-stack task in 2026.
trade: RAG adds a search system you must build, keep fresh and secure, and it adds latency to every question. For a small, stable knowledge base (Anthropic suggests under about 200,000 tokens) putting everything in a cached prompt can be simpler. Sending more chunks is not free either: cost rises and the right chunk can get buried.

myth.m: RAG means the model cannot hallucinate.
myth.r: It reduces it. The model can still misread chunks or fill gaps; grounding instructions, citations and evals keep it honest.

q.s: A legal RAG bot gives confident wrong answers. Logs show the correct document was never retrieved. Where do you focus first?
o: Switch to a bigger LLM
Retrieval: chunking, hybrid search, metadata filters, re-ranking, measured with a retrieval eval set
Raise temperature
Add more system prompt rules
q.e: A model cannot answer from a chunk it never saw.

more: Contextual retrieval (adding document context to chunks)
lab: Build a RAG over 20 markdown docs: chunk by heading, store in pgvector with full-text too, retrieve hybrid top 5, answer with citations.
Write 20 questions with the expected source chunk; measure retrieval hit rate@5 before and after one improvement.

plain:
Retrieval-augmented generation: when a question comes in, first search your own documents for the most relevant passages, then give those passages to the model with the question, and ask it to answer only from them and cite them.

This lets a model answer about your private, recent or specialised data without retraining it.
bridge: It is like an open-book exam. Your code is the assistant who finds the right three pages; the model is the student who writes the answer from them.

walk.title: Answering “Can I work part-time on a student visa?”
steps: Ingestion (once): split legal FAQ documents into chunks by heading, add metadata (source, date), embed and store.
Retrieve: embed the question, run hybrid search, keep the top 5 chunks.
Generate: prompt = rules (“answer only from the sources; cite them; say if not covered”) + the 5 chunks in tags + the question.
The model answers with references like [2], [4]; the UI shows links to those sources.
Evaluate: a test set of 50 questions checks whether the right chunk was retrieved and whether answers stay faithful.

terms: A piece of a document stored for retrieval.
Finding relevant chunks for a question.
Making the model answer from given sources.
A second, more accurate pass to reorder retrieved chunks.
insights: Most bad RAG answers are retrieval failures; check what was retrieved before blaming the model.
Enforce permissions at retrieval time, or users see documents they should not.
Ask for citations; they make answers checkable and reduce invention.

prod.summary: In production, RAG is mostly a search system with an LLM at the end. Seniors measure retrieval separately from generation, enforce permissions at retrieval time, keep the index fresh, require citations, and log what was retrieved for every answer so bad answers can be debugged.
checklist: Retrieval runs with the end user's permissions (tenant, groups, document ACLs), never with a service account that can see everything.
Every answer logs the question, the retrieved chunk IDs and the cited IDs, so a bad answer can be traced to retrieval or generation.
There is a labelled set of questions with the expected source chunk; recall@k is tracked on every chunking, model or index change.
Chunks carry metadata (source, section, updated_at) and include enough context to stand alone (heading path or a short generated summary).
Deletes and edits reach the index quickly (a deleted document must stop being retrievable).
The prompt says to answer only from sources, cite them, and say “not found”; the UI shows the cited sources.
Retrieved text is treated as untrusted input: documents can contain injected instructions.
numbers: Anthropic's contextual retrieval study: adding chunk context reduced top-20 retrieval failures by 35%; with contextual BM25 by 49%; with re-ranking as well by 67% (5.7% → 1.9%).
Anthropic suggests that a knowledge base under about 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages) can simply go in the prompt (with caching) instead of building RAG.
The generated context added to each chunk in that study was typically 50–100 tokens.
failures: A user sees a summary of an HR document they have no access to.

Retrieval ran without permission filters, and the model summarised what it was given. Filter by the user's ACL inside the search query, and add a test that a restricted document never appears for an unprivileged user.
Confident wrong answers; the logs show the correct document was not in the top 5.
A retrieval failure, not a model failure. Check chunking (was the answer split across chunks?), add keyword search, a re-ranker, or more candidates before re-ranking. Measure with recall@k.
Users get answers based on a policy that was replaced last week.
Stale index: the old version is still indexed or ranks higher. Re-index on change, delete old versions, and filter or boost by updated_at.
The answer cites [7], but only 5 sources were sent.
The model invented a citation. Check cited IDs against the sources in code; drop or flag invalid citations, and track the rate.
Answers get worse after raising top-k from 5 to 30.
More chunks add noise and cost; relevant text gets buried. Retrieve wide (e.g. 50), re-rank, and send only the best few.

qs.s: Your RAG eval reports two numbers: retrieval recall@5 = 62% and faithfulness (answers supported by the given chunks) = 97%. Users complain about wrong answers. Where do you invest first?
o: Retrieval: chunking, hybrid search, re-ranking
A bigger generation model
Stricter prompt rules for faithfulness
Lower temperature
qs.e: The model is faithful to what it gets, but 38% of the time it does not get the right chunk. Improving generation cannot fix chunks that were never retrieved.

qs.s: Your company's whole help center is about 120,000 tokens and changes weekly. A teammate proposes a vector DB, a chunking pipeline and a re-ranker. What is a simpler option to evaluate first?
o: Fine-tune a model on the help center
Put the whole help center in a cached prompt prefix and test answer quality and cost
Use keyword search only
Answer without any documents
qs.e: Below roughly 200k tokens, long context with prompt caching can beat a RAG pipeline on simplicity and quality. Measure cost per question with caching; build RAG only if it is needed.

qs.s: A customer deletes a confidential document in your app. An hour later, your assistant still quotes it. What is the root cause?
o: The LLM memorised the document
The prompt cache stored it
The document's chunks are still in the vector index; deletes are not propagated to retrieval
The browser cached the answer
qs.e: The API is stateless and does not learn from your calls. If deleted content appears, it is still being retrieved. Deletes must remove or tombstone chunks in the index immediately; this is also a privacy requirement.

qs.s: Read the trace of one wrong answer. What is the root cause and fix?

code.title: rag-trace.log
code.src:
question: "How many vacation days after 3 years?"
retrieved:
  [1] hr-policy-2022#12   updated=2022-03-01  score=0.83
  [2] hr-policy-2025#40   updated=2025-01-15  score=0.81
  [3] faq#3               updated=2024-06-10  score=0.79
answer: "You get 15 days after 3 years [1]."
expected: 18 days (2025 policy)

o: Both policy versions are indexed and the old one ranks higher. Remove or mark superseded versions so they are filtered out, and prefer newer documents when versions overlap
The model misread chunk [2]; use a bigger model
Top-k is too small; retrieve 30 chunks
Lower the similarity threshold to 0.7
qs.e: The model answered faithfully from source [1], which is outdated. This is an index freshness problem, not a generation problem. Ingestion must delete or mark replaced versions, and retrieval can filter by status or boost by updated_at. More chunks would add the stale one anyway.

qs.s: Users in small teams often get “I could not find this in our documents” although the document exists and they can open it. Read the retrieval code. Why?

code.title: retrieve.ts

o: It leaks restricted documents to the model
canRead is too slow, so it times out

The permission filter runs after limit: 5: the top 5 often belong to other teams, so nothing is left. Put the ACL filter inside the search query (with iterative index scans) so the limit applies to allowed rows
The similarity scores are too low for small teams
qs.e: Filtering after the limit is safe but starves results for users who can see only a small part of the corpus. Filtering inside the query keeps both security and recall. The tempting answer “it leaks restricted documents” is wrong: the code does filter before returning; the bug is recall, not a leak.

qs.s: Each RAG answer sends 8 chunks of about 800 tokens, a 1,500-token system prompt and a 200-token question. At 20,000 questions a day, about how many input tokens is that per day?
o: About 16 million
About 1.6 million
About 8 million
About 162 million
qs.e: 8 × 800 + 1,500 + 200 = 8,100 tokens per question; × 20,000 = 162 million input tokens a day. Retrieved chunks dominate. Caching the system prompt helps a little; sending fewer, better chunks (re-rank, then keep 3–5) helps much more.

qs.s: Answers about plan fees are often wrong. The fees are in a large table, and fixed-size 500-token chunks split the table header from many of its rows. What is the best fix?
o: Increase top-k so all parts of the table come back
Chunk by structure: keep tables whole where possible, or repeat the header row and the section heading in every table chunk so each chunk stands alone
Ask the model to “guess the column names”
Convert the table to an image
qs.e: A row without its header (“12 | 5 | yes”) has no meaning for the retriever or the model. Structure-aware chunking and adding context (heading path, header row) make chunks self-contained. More top-k adds noise and still may not reunite header and row.

interview.q: Design a RAG assistant over a company's wiki and shared drives, where every user may see different documents.
answer: Ingestion: connectors per source, structure-aware chunking, metadata (source, path, updated_at, ACL groups), embeddings plus a keyword index; deletes and permission changes propagate within minutes.
Retrieval runs with the end user's identity: ACL filter inside the query, hybrid search, re-rank, keep the best 3–6 chunks.
Generation: chunks in numbered tags, answer only from sources, cite, say “not found”; citations checked in code against what was sent.
Logging: question, retrieved IDs, cited IDs, prompt version, so each bad answer can be classified as retrieval or generation failure.
Evals: labelled questions with expected sources (recall@k) plus faithfulness checks; a test that a restricted document never appears for an unprivileged user.
Security: retrieved text is untrusted (injection), the assistant has no write tools in this flow.
followups: How do you handle a document whose permissions change?
How fresh must the index be, and how do you guarantee it?

interview.q: Your RAG answers are wrong about 15% of the time. How do you find out why, and what do you fix first?
answer: Take 50–100 bad answers from logs and classify each: right chunk not retrieved, retrieved but ranked low and cut, retrieved but misread, or the documents themselves are wrong or outdated.
Measure retrieval separately (recall@k on a labelled set) from generation (faithfulness given the chunks).
If retrieval is the problem: chunking, hybrid search, re-ranker, query rewriting, metadata filters, freshness.
If generation is the problem: clearer grounding rules, fewer and better chunks, citations, a stronger model for this route.
Fix the biggest bucket first, add the failures to the eval set, and re-measure.
followups: What if the documents contradict each other?
How do you measure faithfulness automatically?

interview.q: When would you NOT build RAG?
answer: When the whole knowledge base is small: Anthropic suggests that under about 200,000 tokens it can go straight into a cached prompt, which is simpler and often more accurate.
When the data is structured (orders, balances, inventory): give the model a tool or a SQL view, not embeddings of rows.
When the goal is style or format, not knowledge: examples in the prompt (or fine-tuning) fit better.
When answers must be exact and auditable from one source of truth: a deterministic lookup beats retrieval plus generation.
Trade-off: long context costs more tokens per call; RAG adds a pipeline to build, secure and keep fresh.
followups: How would you measure whether long context beats RAG for your data?
Can you combine both?
