one: An open protocol for exposing tools, resources and prompts to AI applications in a standard way, so one integration works across many AI clients.
an: USB for AI tools: build the plug once, and any compatible assistant can use your device.
how: An MCP server exposes tools (actions the model can call), resources (data to read) and prompts (templates for users). The host is the AI application (Claude apps, IDEs, agent frameworks); it runs one client per server connection and offers the server's features to the model.

Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0. Standard transports: stdio (the host starts the server as a local subprocess) and Streamable HTTP (each message is an HTTP POST to one endpoint; replies come as JSON or a request-scoped SSE stream).

The 2026-07-28 spec revision makes MCP stateless. There is no initialize handshake and no Mcp-Session-Id. Every request carries its protocol version and client capabilities, and servers implement server/discover. If a server needs more input (for example, a question to the user), it returns an “input required” result, and the client retries the request with the answer. Sampling and Roots are deprecated.

Remote servers use OAuth 2.1. The server is a resource server: it publishes Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728), answers missing, invalid or expired tokens with 401, and accepts only tokens issued for itself (audience check, RFC 8707). Local stdio servers take credentials from the environment instead.
Your server is an API: authenticate users, authorise every tool call, validate inputs, rate-limit, sanitise outputs, and log.
why: Companies now ship MCP servers next to their REST APIs so customers' AI assistants can use their product. Full-stack devs build these.
trade: Installing third-party MCP servers grants them real access; review them like any dependency. Tool descriptions themselves can carry injection.

myth.r: It is a protocol for connecting models' host applications to external tools and data.

q.s: You build a remote MCP server exposing your SaaS's invoice data. What must it enforce?
o: Nothing; the AI client handles it
Per-user authentication (e.g. OAuth) and authorisation on every tool call, like any API
Only HTTPS
Only rate limits
q.e: An MCP server is a public API surface. Same rules apply.

lab: Build a minimal MCP server with the official TypeScript SDK exposing one read-only tool over your own data; connect it to Claude Desktop or Claude Code and call it.

plain:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard way to connect AI assistants to tools and data. You build one MCP server for your product, and any assistant that supports MCP (Claude apps, IDEs, agent frameworks) can use it.

It is like a universal plug, so you do not build a separate integration for every AI client.
bridge: It is to AI assistants what a REST API is to frontends: a defined interface others can call. And like a REST API, it must authenticate users and check permissions.

walk.title: Letting a user's assistant read their invoices
steps: You build an MCP server exposing a tool list_invoices(status) and get_invoice(id).
A customer connects it in their AI assistant; the server uses OAuth so they log in to your product.
The customer asks the assistant: “Which invoices are overdue?”
The assistant calls list_invoices({ status: 'overdue' }); your server checks the token and returns only that customer's invoices.
The assistant answers using real data from your product.

terms: A service that exposes tools, resources and prompts via the protocol.
The host is the AI application; inside it, a client is the connector to one server.
An action the model can call / data it can read.
How client and server talk: stdio (local subprocess) or Streamable HTTP (remote).
Hints like readOnlyHint or destructiveHint for the client UI. Not a security control.
insights: An MCP server is a public API surface; apply the same auth and authorisation rules.
Installing third-party MCP servers gives them real access; review them like dependencies.
Clear tool descriptions matter as much as clear API docs; the model reads them to decide.

prod.summary: In production, a remote MCP server is a public API that AI clients call on behalf of your users. Seniors implement proper OAuth (audience-checked tokens, scopes), authorise every tool call from the token rather than from model-chosen arguments, design tools and descriptions for a model reader, keep results small, and review third-party servers like any dependency with production access.
checklist: Remote server: OAuth 2.1 resource server with Protected Resource Metadata, a 401 + WWW-Authenticate challenge, and audience validation; tokens for other services are rejected, never passed through.
Each tool reads the user/account from the verified token, never from an argument the model supplies.
Scopes are minimal (invoices:read vs invoices:write); write tools ask for more scope only when needed (403 insufficient_scope).
Tool descriptions say what the tool does, when to use it and its limits; results are small and paginated.
Business errors return isError: true with an actionable message; unknown tools and malformed requests return JSON-RPC errors.
HTTP servers validate Host/Origin (DNS-rebinding protection), especially local servers bound to localhost.
Third-party MCP servers are reviewed and pinned like dependencies: what they can access, who publishes them, what their tool descriptions say.
numbers: Current MCP spec revision: 2026-07-28; messages are JSON-RPC 2.0, and the standard transports are stdio and Streamable HTTP.

MCP authorization is based on OAuth 2.1; servers must implement OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728), clients must send the resource parameter (RFC 8707), and Dynamic Client Registration is now deprecated in favour of Client ID Metadata Documents.
MCP spec: tool names should be 1–128 characters (letters, digits, _, -, .), and clients must treat tool annotations as untrusted unless the server is trusted.
MCP TypeScript SDK v2 ships as @modelcontextprotocol/server and @modelcontextprotocol/client and supports both the pre-2026 (initialize handshake) and 2026-07-28 protocol eras.
MCP 2026-07-28: protocol-level sessions and the Mcp-Session-Id header are removed; servers that need state across calls return explicit handles that the client passes back as ordinary tool arguments.
MCP 2026-07-28: SSE resumability is removed; if a response stream breaks, the client re-sends the request with a new request ID, so tools with side effects should be idempotent.
MCP 2026-07-28: servers SHOULD return tools/list in a deterministic order, which also helps LLM prompt-cache hit rates.
failures: A user's assistant lists invoices from another customer's account.
The tool used an account_id argument chosen by the model. Read the account from the verified token in the handler, and ignore or remove ID arguments that select whose data to read.
Your MCP server accepts a token issued for a different API of your company.
Missing audience validation (and possibly token passthrough to upstream APIs). Check that the token's audience is this server's canonical URI; never forward the client's token downstream.
After installing a community MCP server, the agent starts reading ~/.ssh files.

Tool descriptions or results from that server carried injected instructions, and the host auto-approved tools. Review third-party servers, deny auto-approval for sensitive tools, and run servers with least privilege.
The model calls search on the wrong server and gets confusing results.
Two connected servers expose tools with the same name. Use specific names (invoices_search) and clear descriptions; hosts may prefix names with the server ID.
Responses are slow and context overflows after one list_records call.
The tool returns thousands of rows. Paginate with a cursor, cap results, and return only the fields the model needs.

code.title: Remote MCP server (TS SDK v2): audience-checked bearer auth and token-scoped data
code.note: Two lines matter most: the catch that converts any verification failure into OAuthError(InvalidToken) (otherwise clients get a 500 instead of the 401 the spec requires), and the where: { accountId } that scopes data by the token. The server must also serve its Protected Resource Metadata document at the advertised URL (the SDK's oauthMetadataResponse helper does this).

qs.s: Your MCP tool is get_invoices({ account_id }). The handler checks that the request has a valid OAuth token. What is still wrong?
o: Nothing; a valid token means the user is allowed
The tool should use stdio instead
The account comes from the model's argument, so a valid user can read any account; derive it from the token instead
The tool needs a readOnlyHint annotation
qs.e: Authentication is not authorisation. A model can be told (or tricked) to pass any ID. Bind data access to the identity in the verified token. Annotations are UI hints, not access control.

qs.s: Your remote MCP server receives a valid, unexpired JWT from your company's identity provider, but it was issued for your billing API, not for the MCP server. What should the server do?
o: Reject it with 401: the audience must be this MCP server
Accept it; it is signed by the same identity provider
Accept it and forward it to the billing API
Accept it only for read-only tools
qs.e: The MCP spec requires servers to validate that tokens were issued for them (audience) and forbids passing tokens through. Accepting tokens minted for other services enables confused-deputy attacks.

qs.s: You build a small internal tool that only runs on developers' laptops inside Claude Code or an IDE. Which setup fits best?
o: A remote Streamable HTTP server with full OAuth
A stdio server started by the host as a subprocess, with credentials from the environment
A REST API with a Swagger file instead of MCP
A browser extension
qs.e: stdio is the standard local transport: the host launches the server, and the spec says stdio servers should get credentials from the environment rather than run the OAuth flow. Remote HTTP with OAuth is for hosted, multi-user servers.

qs.s: An MCP client with an expired token gets HTTP 500 from your server and never shows the user a login prompt. Read the verifier. Why?

code.title: auth.ts

o: Expired tokens must be refreshed by the server, not rejected

The verifier lets a plain Error escape. The SDK maps only OAuthError with invalid_token to 401 + WWW-Authenticate; anything else becomes 500. Catch and re-throw as OAuthError(OAuthErrorCode.InvalidToken, …)
requiredScopes causes a 500 when the token has no scopes
The audience check should be removed for expired tokens
qs.e: The MCP spec says invalid or expired tokens MUST get a 401, and the client starts the OAuth flow from that 401's challenge. The SDK's bearer helper turns a non-OAuth error into 500 server_error, which clients treat as a server failure. Servers never refresh a client's token.

qs.s: A new MCP client cannot connect: it says it cannot find where to log in. Read the response your server sends to an unauthenticated request. What is missing?

code.title: response
code.src:
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"
Content-Type: application/json

{"error":"invalid_token","error_description":"Missing Authorization header"}

o: The status should be 403, not 401
The body must be JSON-RPC, not OAuth JSON
A Location header pointing to the login page

The Protected Resource Metadata link: resource_metadata="https://mcp.acme.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp" (and ideally scope=) in WWW-Authenticate, plus that metadata document served at the URL
qs.e: MCP servers must implement Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728), and clients discover the authorization server through it, typically from the resource_metadata parameter in the 401 challenge. 403 is for insufficient scope; a redirect does not work for API clients.

qs.s: Your MCP server kept the user's “selected project” in memory keyed by Mcp-Session-Id. You upgrade to the 2026-07-28 protocol. What is the right redesign?
o: Keep it; the header is optional but still sent
Store it in a cookie

Sessions are gone. Return an explicit handle (for example, project_id from select_project) that the model passes back as a tool argument, and check on every call that the token's user may use that project
Use the client's IP address as the session key
qs.e: The 2026-07-28 revision removes protocol-level sessions and the Mcp-Session-Id header; servers needing cross-call state use explicit handles passed as ordinary tool arguments. Because the model supplies the handle, authorisation must still come from the token. IP addresses and cookies are not reliable identities for MCP clients.

qs.s: A team designs a new MCP server that calls sampling/createMessage so it can use the client's model to summarise data. What should you tell them?
o: Sampling is deprecated in the 2026-07-28 spec; new implementations should not adopt it. Call an LLM provider API directly from the server instead
Good design: sampling is the standard way for servers to use models
Sampling only works over stdio
Use Roots instead of Sampling
qs.e: The 2026-07-28 changelog deprecates Roots, Sampling and Logging, and suggests integrating directly with LLM provider APIs instead of Sampling. Deprecated features still work during a deprecation window of at least 12 months, but new servers should not depend on them. Roots is deprecated too.

interview.q: We want customers' AI assistants to use our product. Walk me through building and securing a remote MCP server.
answer: Pick a small set of task-shaped tools (and read-only resources) with clear descriptions and small, paginated results; deterministic tools/list order.

Auth: OAuth 2.1 resource server; Protected Resource Metadata advertised in the 401 challenge; tokens validated for signature, expiry and audience (this server only); never pass the client's token through to other APIs.
Authorisation per tool from the verified token (account, scopes), never from model-chosen IDs; write tools need extra scopes and return 403 insufficient_scope when missing.
Errors: business errors as tool results with isError: true and an actionable message; protocol errors as JSON-RPC errors.
Operations: Host/Origin validation, rate limits per account, request logging with tool name and account, idempotent side effects (a broken stream means the client re-sends the request).
Trade-off: MCP gives one integration for many AI clients, but it is a new public API surface to version, secure and support.
followups: How do you version tools without breaking existing clients?
What would you rate-limit, and by what key?

interview.q: MCP, plain function calling, or a REST API: when does MCP add value?
answer: Plain function calling is enough when you own both the app and the tools: one product, one model integration.
MCP adds value when many different AI hosts (IDEs, chat apps, agent frameworks) should use the same capability without custom integrations each time.
A REST API is still the source of truth for non-AI clients; an MCP server is often a thin, model-friendly layer over it.
MCP brings a standard for discovery, auth (OAuth with metadata), tool schemas and errors, which helps third parties.
Costs: another surface to secure and maintain, and tool descriptions that compete for the model's attention with other servers' tools.
followups: Would you build MCP for an internal-only tool?
How do you avoid tool-name collisions with other servers?

interview.q: How do you evaluate a third-party MCP server before engineers install it?
answer: Treat it like a dependency with production access: who publishes it, is the source available, how are releases signed and pinned.
Read what it can reach: local files, network, credentials in the environment; run it with least privilege (container, limited env vars, scoped tokens).
Read its tool descriptions and sample outputs for injected instructions; annotations like “read-only” are untrusted hints.
Configure the host so sensitive tools need approval; do not auto-approve everything.
Pin versions and review diffs on upgrade, because a tool description change can change agent behaviour.
followups: What would make you reject a server outright?
How do you handle servers that need broad file-system access?

diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as Customer
  participant H as AI assistant (host)
  participant S as Your MCP server
  participant D as Invoices DB
  H->>S: First request, no token
  S-->>H: 401 + metadata URL
  H->>U: Log in to Acme (OAuth)
  U-->>H: Token for mcp.acme.com
  U->>H: Which invoices are overdue?
  H->>S: list_invoices(overdue) + token
  S->>S: Check signature, expiry, audience
  S->>D: WHERE account = token subject
  D-->>S: This customer's rows only
  S-->>H: JSON-RPC result
  H-->>U: Answer from real data
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the account comes from the verified token, not from an argument the model chose. A 401 with the metadata URL is what lets the client start the login flow.
